summary.title: Code Review in Remote Teams
summary.one_liner: Learn how to run written, asynchronous code reviews on a remote team in a way that builds morale and code quality, by avoiding blunt or personal criticism and favouring praise, questions and agreed standards.
keywords: criticize the code not the coder
avoid accusatory language in code review
linters instead of code review nitpicks
takeaways: Code review serves team culture, morale, learning and knowledge sharing as well as finding bugs and code quality problems.
Avoid blunt, personal, demanding, hyperbolic or passive-aggressive comments, and avoid piling on or acting as a back-seat coder.
Praise specific good parts of the code sincerely, and put a positive summary at the top of the review.
Phrase criticism as questions with reasons (e.g. 'What was the reasoning behind...?') to invite explanation rather than demand changes.
Document coding standards and a checklist up front, let linters handle formatting, and have coder and reviewer design the feature together before review.
summary.summary: The author, a engineer at Hypothesis, shares research on making code reviews pleasant and effective for a fully remote team that reviews code asynchronously through GitHub pull requests. The post lists the aims of code review, then gives a set of "don'ts" covering tone, accusatory or demanding language, back-seat coding, and over-commenting, followed by "do's" such as praising good code, asking questions instead of making statements, using checklists and documented coding standards, and letting tools handle style. It closes by recommending a shared team guide and early collaboration between coder and reviewer. Many points are sourced from quoted authors such as Robert Bogue, Erik Dietrich and Daniel Bader.
